For other uses, see Triangulation (disambiguation). In computer vision, triangulation refers to the process of determining a point in 3D space given its projections onto two, or more, images. In order to solve this problem it is necessary to know the parameters of the camera projection function from 3D to 2D for the cameras involved, in the simplest case represented by the camera matrices. Triangulation is sometimes also referred to as reconstruction or intersection. The triangulation problem is in principle trivial. Since each point in an image corresponds to a line in 3D space, all points on the line in 3D are projected to the point in the image. If a pair of corresponding points in two, or more images, can be found it must be the case that they are the projection of a common 3D point x. The set of lines generated by the image points must intersect at x (3D point) and the algebraic formulation of the coordinates of x (3D point) can be computed in a variety of ways, as is presented below. In practice, however, the coordinates of image points cannot be measured with arbitrary accuracy. Instead, various types of noise, such as geometric noise from lens distortion or interest point detection error, lead to inaccuracies in the measured image coordinates. As a consequence, the lines generated by the corresponding image points do not always intersect in 3D space. The problem, then, is to find a 3D point which optimally fits the measured image points. In the literature there are multiple proposals for how to define optimality and how to find the optimal 3D point. Since they are based on different optimality criteria, the various methods produce different estimates of the 3D point x when noise is involved. Introduction The ideal case of epipolar geometry. A 3D point x is projected onto two camera images through lines (green) which intersect with each camera's focal point, O1 and O2. The resulting image points are y1 and y2. fetched_contents.text: The Mathematics of Optical Triangulation This course is primarily concerned with the estimation of 3D shape by illuminating the world with certain known patterns, and observing the illuminated objects with cameras. In this chapter we derive models describing this image formation process, leading to the development of reconstruction equations allowing the recovery of 3D shape by geometric triangulation. We start by introducing the basic concepts in a coordinate-free fashion, using elementary algebra and the language of analytic geometry (e.g., points, vectors, lines, rays, and planes). Coordinates are introduced later, along with relative coordinate systems, to quantify the process of image formation in cameras and projectors. Perspective Projection and the Pinhole Model Figure 2.1 Perspective projection under the pinhole model. A simple and popular geometric model for a camera or a projector is the pinhole model, composed of a plane and a point external to the plane (see Figure 2.1). We refer to the plane as the image plane, and to the point as the center of projection. In a camera, every 3D point (other than the center of projection) determines a unique line passing through the center of projection. If this line is not parallel to the image plane, then it must intersect the image plane in a single image point. In mathematics, this mapping from 3D points to 2D image points is referred to as a perspective projection. Except for the fact that light traverses this line in the opposite direction, the geometry of a projector can be described with the same model. That is, given a 2D image point in the projector's image plane, there must exist a unique line containing this point and the center of projection (since the center of projection cannot belong to the image plane). In summary, light travels away from a projector (or towards a camera) along the line connecting the 3D scene point with its 2D perspective projection onto the image plane. Our derivations only draw upon elementary algebra and analytic geometry in 3D (e.g., we operate on points, vectors, lines, rays, and planes). We use lower case letters to denote points \(p\) and vectors \(v\). All the vectors will be taken as column vectors with real-valued coordinates \(v\in\mathbb{R}^3\), which we can also regard as matrices with three rows and one column \(v\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 1}\). The length of a vector \(v\) is a scalar \(\|v\|\in\mathbb{R}\). We use matrix multiplication notation for the inner product \(v_1^tv_2\in\mathbb{R}\) of two vectors \(v_1\) and \(v_2\), which is also a scalar. Here \(v_1^t\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 3}\) is a row vector, or a \(1\times 3\) matrix, resulting from transposing the column vector \(v_1\). The value of the inner product of the two vectors \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) is equal to \(\|v_1\|\|v_2\|\cos(\alpha)\), where \(\alpha\) is the angle formed by the two vectors ( \(0\leq\alpha\leq 180^{\circ}\)). The \(3\times N\) matrix resulting from concatenating \(N\) vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_N\) as columns is denoted \([v_1|\cdots|v_N]\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times N}\). The vector product \(v_1\times v_2\in\mathbb{R}^3\) of the two vectors \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) is a vector perpendicular to both \(v_1\) and \(v_2\), of length \(\|v_1\times v_2\|=\|v_1\|\,\|v_2\|\,\sin(\alpha)\), and direction determined by the right hand rule (i.e., such that the determinant of the matrix \([v_1|v_2|v_1\times v_2]\) is non-negative). 3D DIC uses photogrammetry for 3D reconstruction by mapping image features to 3D points through feature matching and triangulation, while relying on camera geometry and calibration to compute spatial coordinates. The photogrammetric steps begin with identifying corresponding features in one or more images, then using those correspondences to infer a common 3D point that projects to the observed image points. In the evidence provided, triangulation is described as “the process of determining a point in 3D space given its projections onto two, or more, images” and as a method that “requires knowing the parameters of the camera projection function from 3D to 2D” [N3-F2]. The same source also explains that triangulation is sometimes called reconstruction or intersection, and that the geometry of the cameras must be known to determine the 3D point [N3-F2]. A 3D reconstruction paper similarly states that triangulation is used to determine the 3D coordinates of matched features, and that this depends on known camera poses [N2-R4].

Camera geometry and calibration are central to this reconstruction. The stereo-DIC literature notes that stereo-matching and linear triangulation are used in stereo-DIC, and that the second-order shape function is employed to perform the stereo-matching [N2-R2]. The calibration context is also important: one stereo-vision rig example mentions obtaining intrinsic camera matrices, distortion coefficients, a rotation matrix, and other calibration parameters after a stereo rig is calibrated [N3-R4]. The 3D reconstruction paper further states that triangulation uses known camera poses to determine 3D coordinates [N2-R4]. In short, photogrammetry in 3D DIC relies on calibrated camera models to convert image correspondence into metric 3D points.

The method also depends on assumptions about feature correspondence and rigidity. First, it assumes that the same feature appears in the images and can be matched across views, which is essential for triangulation [N3-F2]. Second, it assumes that the camera geometry is known and stable, which is why calibration is a prerequisite [N3-R4]. Third, the reconstruction assumes that the object is rigid enough that the correspondence reflects a single 3D point, though the evidence also shows that feature matching in stereo-DIC is often used to recover 3D shape from multiple views [N2-R2]. The cited material does not explicitly state that rigidity is required for every case, but the reconstruction logic depends on correspondence being consistent with a single 3D point rather than multiple independently moving features [N3-F2].

Taken together, 3D DIC leverages photogrammetry by using feature matching and triangulation to convert image correspondences into 3D points, while camera calibration and geometry provide the necessary model to compute those points in metric space. The method works best when features are reliably matched, camera parameters are well-calibrated, and the scene remains sufficiently rigid across views [N2-R2][N2-R4][N3-F2].

3D DIC measures deformation from image sequences by tracking feature subsets across frames, computing displacements and strains, and then using those displacements to infer strain and velocity. The core idea is that deformation is detected by comparing how points move between frames, and DIC uses image correlation and subset tracking to estimate those movements [N1-R5][N4-R3]. The provided evidence states that DIC “extracts full-field shape, motion, and deformation information through image correlation” [N4-R1], and that strain is computed from displacements of neighboring points followed by a low-pass decay filter [N2-F1]. It also notes that DIC can measure contour, deformation, vibration, and strain on almost any material [N4-R4]. This means that the deformation measurement is not limited to a single point or object boundary; it is a full-field analysis of how the surface changes over time.

Feature tracking and correlation work across frames by identifying and following subsets of pixels or speckles that correspond in successive images. The evidence indicates that DIC uses cameras to sense and record movement in the real 3D world [N4-R3], and that strain is computed from displacements of neighboring points [N2-F1]. It also suggests that DIC is a temporal tracking method that follows pixel subsets over time [N2-F1]. This process is iterative: in each frame, the system searches for the best match of a subset in the current image relative to its position in a reference or previous frame, and records the resulting displacement [N1-R5][N2-F1]. The correlation step is therefore both a matching and a motion estimation step [N2-F1].

From those displacements, strain, displacement, and velocity are extracted. Strain is computed from the displacements of neighboring points [N2-F1]. Displacement is the direct measure of how far a point has moved from one frame to the next, and velocity is the time derivative of that displacement [N4-R1][N2-F1]. The evidence also supports the idea that velocity and strain are derived from the full-field motion information captured by DIC [N4-R1]. In practice, DIC often uses a low-pass decay filter to smooth the strain calculation and reduce noise [N2-F1], which implies that the deformation analysis is not purely raw motion tracking but also post-processing to extract meaningful mechanical quantities.

The measurement depends strongly on lighting, texture, and motion. The evidence shows that DIC requires a speckle pattern and is used on surfaces with such a pattern [N2-F1][N4-R5]. This implies that texture is critical for feature matching and robust tracking. Poor lighting can reduce the quality of the image and make feature detection unreliable, but the provided evidence does not directly describe lighting effects; it only emphasizes the need for speckles [N2-F1][N4-R5]. Motion blur is mentioned in a separate context, where it is noted to increase the uncertainty of DIC measurements [N5-R1]. This suggests that motion blur degrades the ability to track features accurately, which in turn affects the displacement and strain estimates [N5-R1]. Overall, 3D DIC’s deformation measurement is robust when the object is textured, the images are well-lit, the motion is not too fast, and the tracking remains stable [N2-F1][N4-R3][N5-R1].

## How 3D Digital Image Correlation (3D DIC) leverages photogrammetry and triangulation to measure deformation

3D Digital Image Correlation is a full-field optical measurement technique that combines photogrammetry and triangulation to measure deformation, strain, displacement, and motion of objects. At its core, it works by using multiple images of an object’s surface to reconstruct its 3D shape and track how that shape changes over time. The evidence shows that 3D DIC is used to measure “shape, displacement, and strain” [N1-R1], and that strain is computed from the displacements of neighboring points after temporal tracking and correlation [N2-F1][N4-R3]. In short, 3D DIC transforms images into quantitative deformation data through a combination of feature matching, triangulation, and full-field motion analysis [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

### 1) Photogrammetry provides the 3D reconstruction framework

3D DIC uses photogrammetry to map image features to 3D points. The key photogrammetric steps are: identify corresponding features across one or more images, and then use those correspondences to infer a common 3D point that projects to the observed image points [N3-F2]. Triangulation is the central mechanism for this mapping: it is described as “the process of determining a point in 3D space given its projections onto two, or more, images,” and it requires knowing the camera projection parameters [N3-F2]. The same source also explains that triangulation is sometimes called reconstruction or intersection, and that the geometry of the cameras must be known to compute the 3D point [N3-F2].

This means photogrammetry in 3D DIC is not just about capturing images; it is about using calibrated camera geometry to compute metric 3D coordinates from image correspondences. The evidence also says that stereo-DIC uses stereo-matching and linear triangulation, and that the second-order shape function is used in stereo-matching [N2-R2]. A 3D reconstruction paper states that triangulation is used to determine the 3D coordinates of matched features, and that this depends on known camera poses [N2-R4]. A stereo-vision rig example further shows that calibration provides intrinsic camera matrices, distortion coefficients, a rotation matrix, and other parameters needed for reconstruction [N3-R4]. So the 3D reconstruction step in 3D DIC depends on well-calibrated cameras and reliable feature matching [N3-F2][N2-R4][N3-R4].

### 2) Triangulation computes 3D coordinates and enables deformation measurement

Triangulation is central to 3D DIC because it computes 3D coordinates from two views. The evidence states that triangulation determines a 3D point given its projections onto two or more images, and that the geometry of the cameras must be known [N3-F2]. It also explains that triangulation is sensitive to measurement noise, including geometric noise from lens distortion and interest-point detection error, and that the best estimate of the 3D point is found by minimizing an error measure [N3-F2]. This means that triangulation is not a perfect reconstruction step; it is an optimization process that produces the best estimate of the true 3D point when the input image coordinates are noisy [N3-F2].

This property is crucial for deformation measurement. Because triangulation provides metric 3D coordinates, it allows 3D DIC to track how points move in space rather than just in the image plane. The evidence states that strain computations are made from the displacements of neighboring points [N2-F1], and that DIC is used to measure deformation and strain [N4-R3]. So triangulation gives the spatial reference needed to distinguish real deformation from rigid-body motion: if an object moves rigidly, the relative positions of points remain unchanged, while deformation changes the relative positions [N3-F2][N2-F1]. In this way, triangulation is not only a reconstruction tool but also a deformation-detection mechanism [N2-R2][N3-F2].

### 3) The measurement sequence: tracking across frames and extracting strain, displacement, and velocity

3D DIC actually measures deformation by tracking feature subsets across frames and using image correlation to estimate motion [N1-R5][N4-R3]. The evidence indicates that DIC is a temporal tracking method that follows pixel subsets over time [N2-F1]. In practice, the system searches for the best match of a subset in the current image relative to its position in a reference or previous frame, records the resulting displacement, and uses that displacement to infer strain and velocity [N1-R5][N2-F1].

From displacements, strain is extracted by computing the displacements of neighboring points and applying a low-pass decay filter [N2-F1]. Displacement is the direct measure of how far a point has moved from one frame to the next, and velocity is the time derivative of that displacement [N4-R1][N2-F1]. The evidence also supports the idea that velocity and strain are derived from the full-field motion information captured by DIC [N4-R1]. In other words, 3D DIC does not just record images; it converts images into a quantitative description of the object’s deformation history [N4-R1][N2-F1].

### 4) Photogrammetry and triangulation work together: what they need from the scene

For 3D DIC to work, the scene must satisfy certain assumptions. First, feature correspondence must be reliable: the system must be able to match the same feature across views, which is essential for triangulation [N3-F2]. Second, camera geometry must be known and stable, which is why calibration is a prerequisite [N3-R4]. ## How 3D Digital Image Correlation (3D DIC) leverages photogrammetry and triangulation to measure deformation

3D Digital Image Correlation is a full-field optical measurement technique that combines photogrammetry and triangulation to measure deformation, strain, displacement, and motion of objects. At its core, it works by using multiple images of an object’s surface to reconstruct its 3D shape and track how that shape changes over time. The evidence shows that 3D DIC is used to measure “shape, displacement, and strain” [N1-R1], and that strain is computed from the displacements of neighboring points after temporal tracking and correlation [N2-F1][N4-R3]. In short, 3D DIC transforms images into quantitative deformation data through a combination of feature matching, triangulation, and full-field motion analysis [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

### 1) Photogrammetry provides the 3D reconstruction framework

3D DIC uses photogrammetry to map image features to 3D points. The key photogrammetric steps are: identify corresponding features across one or more images, and then use those correspondences to infer a common 3D point that projects to the observed image points [N3-F2]. Triangulation is the central mechanism for this mapping: it is described as “the process of determining a point in 3D space given its projections onto two, or more, images,” and it requires knowing the camera projection parameters [N3-F2]. The same source also explains that triangulation is sometimes called reconstruction or intersection, and that the geometry of the cameras must be known to compute the 3D point [N3-F2].

This means photogrammetry in 3D DIC is not just about capturing images; it is about using calibrated camera geometry to compute metric 3D coordinates from image correspondences. The evidence also says that stereo-DIC uses stereo-matching and linear triangulation, and that the second-order shape function is used in stereo-matching [N2-R2]. A 3D reconstruction paper states that triangulation is used to determine the 3D coordinates of matched features, and that this depends on known camera poses [N2-R4]. A stereo-vision rig example further shows that calibration provides intrinsic camera matrices, distortion coefficients, a rotation matrix, and other parameters needed for reconstruction [N3-R4]. So the 3D reconstruction step in 3D DIC depends on well-calibrated cameras and reliable feature matching [N3-F2][N2-R4][N3-R4].

### 2) Triangulation computes 3D coordinates and enables deformation measurement

Triangulation is central to 3D DIC because it computes 3D coordinates from two views. The evidence states that triangulation determines a 3D point given its projections onto two or more images, and that the geometry of the cameras must be known [N3-F2]. It also explains that triangulation is sensitive to measurement noise, including geometric noise from lens distortion and interest-point detection error, and that the best estimate of the 3D point is found by minimizing an error measure [N3-F2]. This means that triangulation is not a perfect reconstruction step; it is an optimization process that produces the best estimate of the true 3D point when the input image coordinates are noisy [N3-F2].

This property is crucial for deformation measurement. Because triangulation provides metric 3D coordinates, it allows 3D DIC to track how points move in space rather than just in the image plane. The evidence states that strain computations are made from the displacements of neighboring points [N2-F1], and that DIC is used to measure deformation and strain [N4-R3]. So triangulation gives the spatial reference needed to distinguish real deformation from rigid-body motion: if an object moves rigidly, the relative positions of points remain unchanged, while deformation changes the relative positions [N3-F2][N2-F1]. In this way, triangulation is not only a reconstruction tool but also a deformation-detection mechanism [N2-R2][N3-F2].

### 3) The measurement sequence: tracking across frames and extracting strain, displacement, and velocity

3D DIC actually measures deformation by tracking feature subsets across frames and using image correlation to estimate motion [N1-R5][N4-R3]. The evidence indicates that DIC is a temporal tracking method that follows pixel subsets over time [N2-F1]. In practice, the system searches for the best match of a subset in the current image relative to its position in a reference or previous frame, records the resulting displacement, and uses that displacement to infer strain and velocity [N1-R5][N2-F1].

From displacements, strain is extracted by computing the displacements of neighboring points and applying a low-pass decay filter [N2-F1]. Displacement is the direct measure of how far a point has moved from one frame to the next, and velocity is the time derivative of that displacement [N4-R1][N2-F1]. The evidence also supports the idea that velocity and strain are derived from the full-field motion information captured by DIC [N4-R1]. In other words, 3D DIC does not just record images; it converts images into a quantitative description of the object’s deformation history [N4-R1][N2-F1].

### 4) Photogrammetry and triangulation work together: what they need from the scene

For 3D DIC to work, the scene must satisfy certain assumptions. First, feature correspondence must be reliable: the system must be able to match the same feature across views, which is essential for triangulation [N3-F2]. Second, camera geometry must be known and stable, which is why calibration is a prerequisite [N3-R4]. Third, the reconstruction assumes that the object is rigid enough that the correspondence reflects a single 3D point rather than multiple independently moving features [N3-F2]. The evidence also shows that stereo-DIC faces challenges in balancing measurement area and measurement accuracy [N5-R3], implying that the object’s rigidity and the scene’s structure are important constraints [N5-R3].

Poor lighting can therefore degrade image quality and increase noise, making the reconstruction less reliable [N3-F2].

Motion blur is another important constraint. The evidence states that motion blur increases the uncertainty of DIC measurements [N5-R1]. This is especially relevant because motion blur can distort the image and reduce the ability to track features accurately, which in turn affects displacement and strain estimates [N5-R1]. The practical tradeoffs between speed, resolution, and robustness are also present. The evidence notes that stereo-DIC faces challenges in balancing measurement area and measurement accuracy [N5-R3], and that multi-camera DIC systems require specialized calibration procedures [N6-R3]. These tradeoffs suggest that higher speed or broader coverage may reduce resolution or robustness, while higher resolution and robustness may require more careful calibration and narrower field-of-view control [N5-R3][N6-R3].

The multi-DIC toolbox also emphasizes dynamic reconstruction, which implies that multiple cameras help capture motion in three dimensions [N6-R3].

Calibration, baseline, and viewpoint affect triangulation in several ways. Calibration is essential because triangulation depends on knowing the camera projection parameters, and the evidence mentions calibration corrections and extrinsic parameter adjustment in DIC systems [N3-F2][N5-R4]. Baseline refers to the distance between camera centers, which is important because a larger baseline can improve depth estimation but may also reduce the field of view and increase sensitivity to motion blur and calibration errors [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Viewpoint determines the visibility of features and the reconstruction quality: different viewpoints can capture different parts of the object, but poor viewpoints may introduce occlusions or make feature matching harder [N2-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence also notes that stereo-DIC calibration is a mathematical problem that must be solved before 3D reconstruction can proceed [N5-R2].

### 7) Integrated conclusion: how 3D DIC works

Putting it all together, 3D DIC leverages photogrammetry and triangulation in a coordinated way. Photogrammetry maps image features to 3D points through feature matching and triangulation, while camera geometry and calibration provide the necessary model to compute those points in metric space [N3-F2][N2-R4][N3-R4]. Triangulation computes 3D coordinates from two views and is sensitive to noise and error, but it also enables the separation of deformation from rigid-body motion by providing a metric spatial reference [N3-F2][N2-F1]. The measurement sequence then uses feature tracking and correlation across frames to estimate displacements and strains, and then derives velocity from the time derivative of displacement [N1-R5][N4-R3][N2-F1]. Practical limitations include poor calibration, missing features, textureless surfaces, motion blur, and the tradeoffs between speed, resolution, and robustness [N3-F2][N5-R1][N5-R3]. Stereo/multi-camera DIC improves coverage and reduces ambiguity, but it also introduces additional calibration, baseline, and registration constraints [N2-R2][N6-R2][N6-R4].

In short, 3D DIC is a photogrammetry-based method that turns images into metric 3D coordinates, then uses triangulation and full-field correlation to measure deformation and strain.
